title: Hijama vs dry cupping: what actually happens in each
angle: method comparison and questions to ask
summary: A practical comparison of wet cupping and dry cupping, with questions to ask a provider about the booked method.

answer.heading: Hijama is wet cupping, while dry cupping does not pierce the skin
answer.text: NCCIH distinguishes the methods by whether the skin is pierced: dry cupping uses suction without piercing, while wet cupping includes piercing before blood flows into the cup. This clinic’s current catalogue lists wet cupping services.

sections.heading: What dry cupping means
paragraphs: The NCCIH overview describes dry cupping as a method in which a cup creates suction on the skin without piercing it.
That definition identifies the method; it does not establish a promised outcome.

sections.heading: What wet cupping or hijama means
paragraphs: In the same independent overview, wet cupping involves piercing the skin before blood flows into the cup. Hijama is the secondary name this clinic uses for wet cupping.
Ask a provider to name the method attached to a booking rather than assuming all cupping appointments are the same.

title: Hijama vs massage: how to choose sensibly
angle: practice comparison without outcome claims
summary: How hijama and massage differ as practices, and why personal medical questions should be taken to a healthcare professional.

answer.heading: Hijama and massage use different methods
answer.text: Hijama is wet cupping, whereas massage involves manipulating soft tissues. Sincerity publishes wet cupping services and does not list massage, so this comparison explains methods rather than recommending one for an individual.

sections.heading: What hijama involves
paragraphs: NCCIH describes wet cupping as using suction and piercing the skin before blood flows into the cup. The evidence for cupping is limited and the source also describes possible side effects.
Sincerity uses hijama as a secondary name for wet cupping.

sections.heading: What massage involves
paragraphs: The separate NCCIH massage overview describes massage therapy as manipulation of the body’s soft tissues. It is not the same procedure as wet cupping.
Definitions alone do not decide which practice is appropriate for a particular person.

sections.heading: How to choose sensibly
paragraphs: First confirm which service a provider actually offers and read independent information about that method. Sincerity’s published service list contains wet cupping and full spiritual appointments, not massage.
Take personal medical questions to an appropriately qualified healthcare professional rather than relying on a comparison page.

title: How to check whether a hijama clinic is trustworthy
angle: specific questions to ask and evidence to request before booking
summary: A checklist of practical questions and evidence to request when assessing whether a hijama clinic is operating safely and transparently.

answer.heading: Trust comes from specific answers, not broad claims
answer.text: A trustworthy clinic answers questions about practitioners, hygiene process, equipment and consent with specific, verifiable information. Broad claims without supporting evidence should prompt further questions.

sections.heading: Questions to ask about practitioners
paragraphs: Ask for the practitioner's name and role. Sincerity names its practitioners — Sister Aisha Mejri for women and Brother Abu Layla for men — so clients can check they are on the correct booking route.

sections.heading: Questions to ask about hygiene and consent
paragraphs: Ask which items are single-use, how used equipment is disposed of and how consent is handled before the appointment begins. A clinic that cannot answer these clearly is worth approaching with caution.

title: What happens during a wet cupping session?
angle: independent NCCIH definition alongside the clinic's published process
summary: An independent summary of what wet cupping involves, using the NCCIH definition, with a reminder that individual outcomes are not predictable.

answer.heading: Wet cupping involves suction and skin piercing
answer.text: The NCCIH describes wet cupping as a form of cupping in which the skin is pierced before blood flows into the cup. That definition identifies the method; it does not establish a promised individual outcome.

sections.heading: What the clinic can explain
paragraphs: The clinic can describe the steps in the service you booked and answer operational questions. Your practitioner will explain the session before it begins and give you the opportunity to ask questions.

sections.heading: What this guide does not predict
paragraphs: Wet cupping is a complementary therapy. This guide does not claim it will treat, cure or prevent any medical condition. Take individual health questions to a healthcare professional.
